newsitem.title: EGYPT: Angry Arafat rejects Israel's new Hebron plan.
newsitem.headline: Angry Arafat rejects Israel's new Hebron plan.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat angrily rejected on Wednesday a new Israeli plan to divide the West Bank town of Hebron into Arab and Jewish parts.
Arafat angrily waved the plan in the air and described it as a tragedy and more racist than apartheid South Africa. "This blows up the agreement," he told reporters at his Cairo home.
"It's a dangerous operation. It shows Israel's aggressive intentions in Hebron and shows complete and abhorrent racism.
"There's no doubt this plan will cause an outcry not just among Palestinians. It will cause an outcry among Palestinians, in the Arab world and internationally," he added.
He said he had complained about it to Egypt and to the ambassadors of three European Union troika countries -- Ireland, Italy and the Netherlands.
The Israelis gave the Palestinians the plan shortly after midnight on Wednesday, apparently during talks at a Jerusalem hotel.
"I want to inform you about a document which is extremely grave...lest it go on the record internationally that we do not want peace. Peace for us is a strategic option," Arafat said.
He said the plan was in two parts, one dictated to the Palestinians in Arabic and the other written in English.

"I will read to you the Arabic because it's serious and it contains racial discrimination...It divides Hebron into two towns, two separate cities but they (the Israelis) have the right of hot pursuit throughout the town.
"It restricts building and town planning in the following places," he adding, listing streets which he said were used by the Jewish settlers who live in the town.
"What racism! It did not happen even in South Africa. the streets in which Jews walk on foot! This never happened anywhere in the world," he said.
Other points in the plan were:
-- Bus stations would be under complete Israeli control.
-- The Israeli army and police would be present at the Tomb of Patriarchs, a site holy to both Jews and Moslems.
-- The Israelis claimed that Dair al-Arbain, which Arafat described as a mosque built 300 years ago, was not a mosque and was a Jewish synagogue.
- For a distance of between 10 and 50 metres (yards) on either side of the controversial streets there must not be a building more than three metres (10 feet).
-- For a distance of between 50 and 150 metres (yards) on either side of the same streets, buildings should not be higher than six metres (20 feet).

-- The Palestinians could not build schools, hospitals or clubs in parts of the town. "This in spite of the fact in the old city there are 20,000 Arabs and only 126 settlers, three quarters of whom do not sleep in Hebron," Arafat said.

Arafat invoked the memory of late Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, with whom he signed the original Hebron agreement more than a year ago. "I have not forgotten that my partner in peacemaking paid with his life for this peace," he said.
In Jerusalem, Israel Foreign Minister David Levy said it could resolve an impasse with Arafat over Hebron within hours if the Palestinian leader would stop playing games.

"What's needed is for Mr Arafat to stop...travelling from place to place as if he has all the time in the world. And there is no room for these games because the subject is serious," Levy told parliament.
